title: Waiting for the Light: A Bible Study for Advent
subtitle: A five-session study for the four Sundays of Advent and Christmas, on a people in the dark, the comfort of a long-promised God, Mary's song, the Word made flesh, and the Christ who will come again.
summary:
This study is for churches and small groups keeping the four weeks before Christmas, and for anyone for whom December is the hardest month of the year. Its five sessions, one for each Sunday of Advent and one for Christmas, read Isaiah's promise of light to a people under Assyria; God's comfort for exiles in Isaiah 40 and old Simeon's long wait; Mary's yes and her song, in which God brings down the proud and lifts the humble; John's confession, with the Nicene Creed, that the Word became flesh; and the hope of Christ's coming again, for everyone who carries an empty chair into Christmas. Each session is built so a busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question comes with a note on what lies behind it, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice.

This study won't hurry anyone to the manger. Advent waits on purpose, and its waiting is a mercy to the people December's cheer leaves out: the grieving, the lonely, the newly divorced, the poor, and the estranged. It reads Isaiah in his own century before reading him toward Christ, because the promises were first spoken to people in real darkness and are stronger for it. It names the questions faithful Christians still disagree about, and it leaves them open. And it implicates its writer and its leaders, who have also trusted the protections they could see, grown impatient with long waits, and heard Mary's song as good news about someone else's fall. It begins where Advent begins, in the dark, where the promise was first given.
audience: Churches and small groups keeping Advent, households, and anyone for whom December is the hardest month
sessionsLabel: 5 sessions (through Advent, or as 8 or 4 weeks)

sessions.title: A People in the Dark
sessions.aim: To read Isaiah's promise of light first where it was spoken, to an occupied Galilee and a frightened king who had bought protection from Assyria, and only then to follow it to Jesus; and to let the room name the darkness it carries into December, and what it has trusted there, without being hurried toward the light.
sessions.summary:
December puts up its lights in the darkest weeks of the year, and for many people the lights don't reach the dark they're actually in. Advent begins there, with a promise most of us know from Christmas cards and Handel's Messiah: "The people walking in darkness have seen a great light" (Isaiah 9:2). Fewer of us know who first heard it.

Isaiah spoke it in the eighth century BC, while Assyria was swallowing the small kingdoms around Judah. Around 735 BC the kings of Aram and Israel marched on Jerusalem, and King Ahaz, terrified, refused Isaiah's call to trust God. He sent the temple's silver and gold to the king of Assyria with a message: "I am your servant and your son" (2 Kings 16:7). Assyria came, and in 733 and 732 BC it annexed Galilee, the lands of Zebulun and Naphtali, and carried their people away (2 Kings 15:29).

Then Isaiah turns on one word: "Nevertheless" (Isaiah 9:1). The light will rise where the darkness fell, and a child will be born who carries the government on his own shoulders instead of handing it to an empire. More than seven centuries later, Matthew tells of Jesus beginning to preach in that same Galilee and hears the promise coming true (Matthew 4:12-17). This session reads the promise where it was first given, follows it to him, and asks two honest questions: what darkness are we in, and what have we trusted in it?

keyScripture.why: Isaiah promises a great light to the lands Assyria had darkened, and a child-king whose names outrun any king Judah ever had: "Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace" (Isaiah 9:6). Read in its own century, it answers a king who trusted an empire; read toward Christ, it names the one Matthew shows preaching in Galilee.

discussion.q: When you hear "The people walking in darkness have seen a great light" (Isaiah 9:2), what do you picture? What has December, with all its lights, been like for you in recent years?
discussion.behind: Surface the defaults before you teach anything. Some will picture candles and a Christmas card; others a hospital corridor or a first Christmas after a death. Let both be true in the room, and correct no one; the struggling need to hear early that they belong here. Go first, briefly, if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Read Isaiah 7:1-12 and 2 Kings 16:5-9. What was Ahaz afraid of, what did Isaiah ask of him, and what did he do instead?
discussion.behind: Make Ahaz understandable before anyone condemns him. Two armies were at his border; Isaiah offered him a sign, and he refused with pious words and chose the protector he could see. Help the room notice the cost: silver from the house of the LORD, and an empire's king called father.

discussion.q: In Isaiah 9:1-7 the light rises on Zebulun and Naphtali, the land Assyria had darkened, and the child's government will be "upon His shoulders" (Isaiah 9:6). What does that say to an occupied Galilee, and to a king who had laid his kingdom on Assyria's shoulders?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge. Keep the promise in its own century before anyone reaches for Bethlehem. To Galilee it says that the land that went dark will see the light; to Ahaz it says God will give a king who carries his people himself. Notice what it rests on: "The zeal of the LORD of Hosts will accomplish this" (Isaiah 9:7).

discussion.q: Matthew says Jesus made his home in Capernaum, "in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali," to fulfill Isaiah's words (Matthew 4:13-16). What changes when you hear the promise first in Isaiah's day and then watch it arrive in Galilee?
discussion.behind: Reading Isaiah in his own time first doesn't weaken the Christian claim; it shows why the first Christians made it. Be honest that faithful readers differ about how much Isaiah's first hearers understood, and let the question become wonder, not debate.

discussion.q: Ahaz sent his silver to Assyria and called its king his father. Where do you, and where does the church, look for rescue in the dark to powers we can see?
discussion.behind: Move to self-implication, and let it fall on every side: a political savior of either party, money, a family's approval, our own competence, the noise of the season. Churches have traded their witness for access too. No one should leave thinking that only the other party trusts Assyria. Go first.

objections.objection: Christians read Jesus back into Isaiah. Isaiah was talking about his own time, probably about a king like Hezekiah, and Matthew pulled the verses out of context to make them fit.
objections.response: Grant what is true. Isaiah spoke to his own century first, which is why this study reads him there. Jewish interpreters have read the child of Isaiah 9 in more than one way, as a king of Isaiah's own day or as the Messiah still to come, and some read the names themselves as praise of the God who gives the child, as many Hebrew names are. Then weigh what the objection leaves out. The names in Isaiah 9:6 outrun any king Judah had, Hezekiah included. "Mighty God" is used of the LORD himself in the next chapter (Isaiah 10:21), and Hezekiah's own story ends with him showing his treasures to envoys from Babylon (Isaiah 39:2). Matthew doesn't claim that Isaiah ignored his own day. He notices that the light began in the very Galilee that had gone dark, carried by one who bore the authority those names describe. A skeptic doesn't have to accept that claim to see that it isn't careless.

objections.objection: This is too much history. People come to church in December to find hope, not to hear about Assyrian kings and deportations.
objections.response: Grant the concern. People arrive in December hurting, and a lecture is cold comfort, so keep the history brief. But the history is the comfort. Isaiah's promise was first spoken to people under occupation, whose neighbors had been marched off to Assyria and whose king had failed them. A hope that held for them can hold in a hospital room or beside an empty chair. Sentimental hope tends to break in a real December, because it was never built for darkness. The hope Isaiah gave was built for exactly that.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What darkness are you carrying into this December that the people around you can't see, and what have you been trusting to keep it at bay?
sessions.practice: Each evening this week, light one candle or sit by one lamp and read Isaiah 9:2-7 aloud. Before you read, name to God one place of darkness in your life or in the world, plainly. After you read, name one thing you have trusted in his place. Don't hurry to resolve either. If you live with children, the family Advent devotions at /family/devotions give a household a short reading for each day until Christmas, and they print as a booklet. At the end of the week, write down whether naming the dark changed how you heard the promise.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord God of Hosts, we come to you as a people in the dark. Some of us carry griefs no one else can see. Like Ahaz, we have trusted the protectors we could see, our money, our parties, and our plans, and we have paid for them with what belonged to you. Forgive us, and forgive your church for the times it sent its silver to Assyria. You kept your promise to the land that went dark. Let your light rise on us where our darkness is deepest, and give us patience to wait for it. In the name of Jesus, the light of the world. Amen.
reflection: What darkness am I carrying into this Advent, and have I let myself name it before God?
Where am I most like Ahaz, choosing the protection I can see over a promise I can't?
What does it mean for me that the light rose in the very land that had gone dark?
sessions.teaching:
Begin with December itself. The lights go up in the darkest weeks of the year, and for many people they don't touch the dark they're in: a first Christmas after a funeral, a marriage that ended this year, children who will wake on Christmas morning in another house, test results that haven't come back. Advent doesn't ask any of them to feel festive. It begins where they are, with a promise spoken to a people in the dark.

Most of us know that promise from Christmas cards and Handel's Messiah: "The people walking in darkness have seen a great light; on those living in the land of the shadow of death, a light has dawned" (Isaiah 9:2). Before we read it as a Christmas text, we need to hear it where Isaiah spoke it. His ministry began around 740 BC, "In the year that King Uzziah died" (Isaiah 6:1), just as Assyria under Tiglath-pileser III was becoming a machine of conquest that deported whole peoples.

Around 735 BC the kings of Aram and Israel marched on Jerusalem, and the hearts of King Ahaz and his people "trembled like trees in the forest shaken by the wind" (Isaiah 7:2). God sent Isaiah to him with a word as plain as any in Scripture: "If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all" (Isaiah 7:9). God even offered Ahaz a sign, and he declined it with pious words. Then he did what frightened people do and chose the protector he could see. He sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser: "I am your servant and your son. Come up and save me" (2 Kings 16:7). And he paid with "the silver and gold found in the house of the LORD" (2 Kings 16:8).

Assyria came. In 733 and 732 BC it annexed Galilee, "all the land of Naphtali," and carried the people off as captives (2 Kings 15:29), and in 732 BC it took Damascus. Zebulun and Naphtali, in the far north, were among the first lands of the kingdom to fall, about a decade before Samaria itself. Ahaz had bought his own safety, and his neighbors' land went dark. Isaiah 8 ends there, with a people who "will look to the earth and see only distress and darkness and the gloom of anguish" (Isaiah 8:22).

Then the passage turns on a single word: "Nevertheless" (Isaiah 9:1). The land God humbled in the past he will honor in the future, and Isaiah speaks of it as if it were already done. The oppressor's yoke is shattered "as in the day of Midian" (Isaiah 9:4), when God cut Gideon's army down to three hundred men so that Israel could not boast, "My own hand has saved me" (Judges 7:2). The rescue will be God's, so that no one, least of all a king who trusted Assyria, can claim it.

Then the child: "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given, and the government will be upon His shoulders" (Isaiah 9:6). Hear it against Ahaz, who had laid his kingdom on Assyria's shoulders. The child will be called Wonderful Counselor, where Ahaz took counsel from his fear; Mighty God, a name Isaiah gives the LORD himself in the next chapter (Isaiah 10:21); Everlasting Father, a name that can sting before it heals for anyone raised without a father or by one who did harm; and Prince of Peace, where Ahaz had bought a peace that cost the temple's treasure. And it all rests on God, not on Judah: "The zeal of the LORD of Hosts will accomplish this" (Isaiah 9:7). Faithful readers differ about how much Isaiah's first hearers understood, whether the child was a direct portrait of the Messiah or a promise with a near horizon that its own names overflowed, but no king of Judah came close to bearing those names.

More than seven centuries later, while Rome ruled Galilee through Herod's son Antipas, Jesus made his home in Capernaum, "in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali" (Matthew 4:13), and Matthew heard Isaiah in it: "the people living in darkness have seen a great light" (Matthew 4:16). The light began where the darkness had begun. For Matthew it was a promise kept in the place it named, by the one whose names it gave.

Now stand inside the story. Ahaz was a frightened man who chose the protection he could see, and so do we. Some of us trust a political savior, of whatever party, to keep the dark away. Some trust money, a family's approval, their own competence, or the noise of the season, which keeps the house from getting quiet enough to feel anything. Churches have sent their silver to Assyria too, trading their witness for access and calling the trade wisdom, and the writer and the leader of this study are not exempt. "I am your servant and your son" (2 Kings 16:7) is the prayer of anyone who has decided that God is too slow.

So Advent begins honestly, by naming the dark we're in and what we've trusted there. The light Isaiah promised came because God was zealous for his promise, and no strategy of Judah's brought it; it rose in the very land that had gone dark. Nothing in that promise says the darkness you brought into this room will lift by the twenty-fifth. It says the dark is not where God leaves the story.

scriptureStudy.note: With two armies at the border, Isaiah offers Ahaz not a strategy but a summons: "If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all" (Isaiah 7:9).

Ahaz's message reads like a prayer addressed to the wrong god: "I am your servant and your son. Come up and save me" (2 Kings 16:7). He even copied an altar he saw in Damascus for the temple (2 Kings 16:10).

Tiglath-pileser took "Galilee, including all the land of Naphtali, and he took the people as captives to Assyria" (2 Kings 15:29). This is the darkness behind Isaiah 9:1: a land emptied by deportation.

The darkness is spiritual before it is political: people consult the dead and curse "their king and their God" (Isaiah 8:21). Then comes the turn: "Nevertheless, there will be no more gloom for those in distress" (Isaiah 9:1).
The verbs speak as if the rescue has already happened. The yoke is shattered "as in the day of Midian" (Isaiah 9:4), when God made Gideon's army small so that the victory could only be his.

Four names answer a failed king point by point, and the second, Mighty God, is used of the LORD in Isaiah 10:21. Everything rests on the last line: "The zeal of the LORD of Hosts will accomplish this" (Isaiah 9:7).

Jesus begins his ministry "in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali" (Matthew 4:13), and his first message is the right answer to a great light: "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near" (Matthew 4:17).

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, read Isaiah 7 to 11 as one stretch about kings: Ahaz, who failed the test of faith; a sign named Immanuel; the child of chapter 9; and the shoot from the stump of Jesse who "will judge the poor" with righteousness (Isaiah 11:4). Weigh the honest difficulty that the sign of Isaiah 7:14 is tied to Ahaz's own crisis, for before the child is grown, "the land of the two kings you dread will be laid waste" (Isaiah 7:16). Some Christians read a near sign with a far fulfillment; others read the promise as aimed at the Messiah from the start.

Archaeological surveys of Galilee show a sharp fall in settlement after the Assyrian conquest, the physical trace of a land gone dark. Ask what it means for Christians to read Israel's Scriptures without taking them away from Israel.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose your group meets for the first time on the first Sunday of Advent. A couple with a new baby are bright with the season. A man near the door lost his job in October. A woman whose husband left in the spring keeps her coat on. Ten minutes in, someone says kindly that the group should keep things positive, since it's Christmas, and someone else admits that the season makes him want to skip church until January.

You will feel the pull to side with the cheer, or to rescue the one who is struggling. Do neither. Thank them both. Read Isaiah 9:2 aloud and ask who it was first spoken to, so that the joyful don't have to apologize for their joy and the grieving don't have to perform. Afterward, speak privately with anyone carrying something heavy, and make sure they know where help is.

Use this to show that Advent has room for both, and ask the group which voice they have been this December.

sessions.title: Comfort, and the Long Wait
sessions.aim: To hear Isaiah 40's command to comfort as a word first spoken to exiles whose city lay in ruins, to watch Simeon wait for that comfort and finally hold it in his arms, and to learn a waiting that is neither resignation nor wishful thinking but trust in a God who comes himself.
sessions.summary:
Most of us wait badly, and December makes it harder, because the waits that matter most can't be hurried: the test results, the son who hasn't called, the grief that hasn't lifted, the prayer unanswered for years.

The second Sunday of Advent hears the opening of Isaiah 40: "Comfort, comfort My people," says your God (Isaiah 40:1). These words assume the worst has already happened. Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in 587 or 586 BC and carried many of its people into exile, and the poet of Lamentations said again and again that there was "no one to comfort her" (Lamentations 1:2). Faithful readers differ about how these chapters came to speak into the exile, but they agree on whom they comfort: a worn-out people who said, "My way is hidden from the LORD" (Isaiah 40:27). The comfort is not a mood. It announces that the sin is pardoned and that God himself is coming, as a shepherd who "gathers the lambs in His arms and carries them close to His heart" (Isaiah 40:11).

More than five hundred years after the first exiles went home, an old man named Simeon was still "waiting for the consolation of Israel" (Luke 2:25). When Mary and Joseph brought their infant son to the temple, he took the child in his arms and said he could now die in peace. This session asks how to wait the way Simeon waited: honestly, for a long time, until God comes.

keyScripture.why: God commands comfort for a city that had no one to comfort her, and grounds it in pardon and in his own arrival: "Here is your God!" (Isaiah 40:9). The one who comes rules with a strong arm and carries the lambs close to his heart. In Luke 2:25-32, Simeon, promised that he would not die before he saw the Lord's Christ, waits for that comfort and finally holds it in his arms.

discussion.q: What are you waiting for this December that you can't hurry? Say as much or as little as you want.
discussion.behind: Begin with honesty, not with the text. Some waits are private; people may answer in general terms or pass. Hearing how many kinds of waiting are in the room makes it easier for anyone to admit that theirs has been long. Go first with something true but not heavy.

discussion.q: Read Lamentations 1:2 and then Isaiah 40:1-2. What do you hear in God saying "Comfort" twice (Isaiah 40:1) to a city where there had been "no one to comfort her" (Lamentations 1:2)?
discussion.behind: Let the two passages answer each other. Notice what the comfort rests on: "her iniquity has been pardoned" (Isaiah 40:2). It doesn't pretend the exile was undeserved; it announces that the sentence is over.

discussion.q: In Isaiah 40:9-11 the comfort is a person arriving: "Here is your God!" He rules with a strong arm and carries the lambs close to his heart. Why do we usually want a solution instead, and what is different about God coming himself?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge. We want our circumstances fixed, and God's first answer to the exiles was his own presence. Hold both images together, the ruling arm and the carrying arms, and point ahead to Simeon, who will hold the child who is that shepherd.

discussion.q: Simeon was "waiting for the consolation of Israel" (Luke 2:25), and when it came he still told Mary that "a sword will pierce your soul as well" (Luke 2:35). How can comfort be real and still include sorrow?
discussion.behind: Protect the honesty of the text. Simeon is ready to die in peace, and he still tells a young mother the truth about what her son will cost her. God's comfort doesn't erase sorrow; it gives sorrow a future. Some in your room have been offered comfort that required them to stop grieving. Simeon's didn't.

discussion.q: The exiles said, "My way is hidden from the LORD" (Isaiah 40:27). Where have you stopped waiting and quietly settled? Where has the church been impatient with people whose waiting lasts too long?
discussion.behind: Move to self-implication. Most of us either settle or keep waiting with a bitterness we call patience, and churches are often impatient with the grieving in their second year, the couple still without a child, the parent of a prodigal. You go first, briefly.

objections.objection: Waiting on God is a pious name for doing nothing. People with real problems need to solve them, not sit around hoping for a sign.
objections.response: Grant what is right in it. Scripture has no patience with passivity dressed up as faith, and many problems should be solved: doctors called, debts faced, hard conversations had. But look at the waiting Isaiah 40 describes: voices preparing a road in the wilderness (Isaiah 40:3) and a herald climbing a mountain with good news (Isaiah 40:9). Anna worshiped in the temple "night and day, fasting and praying" (Luke 2:37). This waiting is active. What it refuses is the idea that our limits are the last word, because some things we cannot fix: death, exile, a world gone wrong.

objections.objection: Isaiah 40 was written to exiles twenty-five centuries ago. Applying it to my December is exactly the kind of misuse the first session warned against.
objections.response: Grant the warning; the chapter belongs to the exiles first, and it would be wrong to read "Comfort, comfort" (Isaiah 40:1) as a promise that your circumstances will change by Christmas. But the chapter itself reaches past its first hearers. It promises that "all humanity together will see" the glory of the LORD (Isaiah 40:5). The Gospels hear its wilderness voice in John the Baptist (Mark 1:2-4), and Simeon heard its comfort as his own hope five centuries later. What carries over is not a timetable but a person, because "the word of our God stands forever" (Isaiah 40:8). Read the chapter as theirs first. Then you can receive it as yours without stealing it.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If God spoke tenderly to the place in you that has waited longest, what would you most need him to say?
sessions.practice: Each evening this week, pray Simeon's prayer slowly (Luke 2:29-32); Christians have prayed it at the close of the day for centuries. Before you pray it, name to God the thing you are waiting for. Once during the week, reach out to someone whose long wait others have forgotten: someone grieving a death from a year or two ago, a friend still out of work, a couple still hoping for a child. Don't offer advice or a verse. Tell them you remember. At the end of the week, write down what it was like to pray a prayer of fulfillment while you were still waiting.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord our God, you spoke tenderly to a ruined city and told your people that their hard service was over. Some of us have stopped waiting and quietly settled, and some of us have hurried others through their waiting. Forgive us. You do not grow tired or weary; give power to the faint among us tonight. Teach us to wait as Simeon waited, honest about the sword and sure of the promise, until our eyes see your salvation. Come to us as the shepherd who carries the lambs close to his heart. In the name of Jesus, the consolation of Israel. Amen.
reflection: What am I waiting for that I cannot hurry, and have I told God the truth about how long it has been?
Where have I stopped waiting and settled, and what would it mean for me to start watching again?
Who around me is in a long wait that others have forgotten, and how could I remember them this week?
sessions.teaching:
Most of us are bad at waiting, and we live in a culture that has worked hard to abolish it. But the waits that matter most can't be shortened by money or effort. Someone in this room is waiting for test results, or for a son to call, or for a grief to lift that hasn't lifted. December makes those waits heavier, because everything around us insists that the moment of arrival is already here.

To hear Isaiah 40 rightly, we have to stand where it stands. Jerusalem fell to Babylon in 587 or 586 BC; the temple was burned, and many of Judah's leading families were carried off to Babylonia for decades. Lamentations keeps returning to one line about the ruined city: "there is no one to comfort her" (Lamentations 1:17). Isaiah 40 speaks as though the city's fall has already happened, and faithful readers differ about how: many hold that Isaiah of Jerusalem received these words in the eighth century for a generation not yet born, and many others that a prophet in Isaiah's tradition spoke them near the end of the exile, before Cyrus of Persia took Babylon in 539 BC. On either view the chapter speaks to exiles, and that is where we read it.

Into a world with no comforter, God doubles the word: "Comfort, comfort My people," says your God (Isaiah 40:1). He tells his messengers, "Speak tenderly to Jerusalem," and the Hebrew says, literally, speak to the heart of Jerusalem. Then he gives the reason: "her forced labor has been completed; her iniquity has been pardoned" (Isaiah 40:2). The comfort names the sin and announces that the sentence has been served and the sin forgiven. Comfort that skips the wound is flattery. God's comfort goes to the wound and speaks there.

Then voices rise. One calls for a highway for the LORD in the wilderness, so that "the glory of the LORD will be revealed, and all humanity together will see it" (Isaiah 40:5). Babylon had a great processional way for carrying the images of its gods; this road is for the living God, coming to his people. Another voice asks what there is to cry when "All flesh is like grass," and hears the hinge of the chapter: "The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever" (Isaiah 40:6-8). Babylon was grass too, and in 539 BC it withered.

Then Zion herself climbs a high mountain and calls to the cities of Judah, "Here is your God!" (Isaiah 40:9). The comfort is God arriving in person, as a king whose "arm establishes His rule" (Isaiah 40:10) and as a shepherd who "gathers the lambs in His arms and carries them close to His heart" (Isaiah 40:11). Power without tenderness would terrify the weary, and tenderness without power could not bring anyone home.

The return that began after Cyrus's decree was real and smaller than the poetry; the exiles came back to ruins and foreign rulers. More than five centuries later, with Judea ruled by Rome through Herod, Luke introduces one of those still waiting. Simeon was "righteous and devout," and "He was waiting for the consolation of Israel" (Luke 2:25). In the Greek Old Testament that Luke's readers knew, the comfort of Isaiah 40:1 and the consolation Simeon awaited come from the same family of words; Simeon was waiting for the comfort Isaiah 40 announced. Anna, a widow well along in years, never left the temple and worshiped there night and day (Luke 2:37), and around them were others "waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem" (Luke 2:38).

Then a poor couple, bringing two birds because they could not afford a lamb (Luke 2:24; Leviticus 12:8), carried their son into the temple, and Simeon took the child in his arms. Isaiah had promised a shepherd who carries the lambs in his arms; now an old man carried the shepherd. He prayed: "Sovereign Lord, as You have promised, You now dismiss Your servant in peace. For my eyes have seen Your salvation, which You have prepared in the sight of all people, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel" (Luke 2:29-32). Much of it is Isaiah's language (Isaiah 40:5; 49:6; 52:10). Then he told Mary the truth: "a sword will pierce your soul as well" (Luke 2:35). The consolation was real, and it gave sorrow a future without erasing it.

So Advent teaches a particular kind of waiting, different both from resignation, the exiles' complaint that "my claim is ignored by my God" (Isaiah 40:27), and from wishful thinking, which has nothing underneath it. Simeon waited on a promise from someone trustworthy, with his eyes open, among God's people. "Those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength" (Isaiah 40:31) was first spoken to exhausted exiles who believed God had lost track of them.

We have to stand inside this. Most of us stop waiting and settle, and call it maturity, or keep waiting with a bitterness we call patience. And churches hurry the grieving and the childless toward comfort because their waiting makes us uncomfortable, which is a failure of love whatever we call it. Some in this room will still be waiting after Christmas, and the promise is no less true for them, because God's comfort is not finally a change of circumstances. It is God himself, coming.

scriptureStudy.note: The ruined city weeps: "For there is no one nearby to comfort me, no one to revive my soul" (Lamentations 1:16). Isaiah 40 answers that refrain with God's own doubled word.
Comfort rests on pardon: the city's "iniquity has been pardoned" (Isaiah 40:2). God declares the exile finished and tells his messengers to speak to the heart of a people who had heard only judgment.

A road for God in the wilderness, with every valley raised and every mountain lowered. The Gospels hear this voice in John the Baptist (Mark 1:2-4; Luke 3:4-6), who prepared the way for the LORD himself.
The herald's question is honest despair: why cry out when people wither like grass? The answer doesn't deny the withering; it sets beside it "the word of our God" that "stands forever" (Isaiah 40:8).
The good news is a person: "Here is your God!" (Isaiah 40:9). He rules with a strong arm and carries the lambs close to his heart, power and tenderness in a single coming.

The exiles' complaint is kept in the text: "My way is hidden from the LORD, and my claim is ignored by my God" (Isaiah 40:27). God answers with who he is, the Creator who "will not grow tired or weary" (Isaiah 40:28).

Simeon waits for "the consolation of Israel" (Luke 2:25), holds the child, and prays Isaiah's hopes back to God. Then he tells Mary what it will cost her. His comfort is honest enough to include the sword.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, follow Simeon's prayer through the church's history. Christians have prayed it at the close of the day for centuries, and it is often called the Nunc Dimittis, from its first words in Latin, now you dismiss. Late in 1943, Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote from his cell in Tegel prison in Berlin that a prison cell, where a person waits and hopes and cannot open a door that opens only from outside, is not a bad picture of Advent. Charles Wesley's Advent hymn Come, Thou Long Expected Jesus calls Christ Israel's strength and consolation, Simeon's word.

Then weigh the question this session leaves open, how Isaiah 40 came to speak into the exile, using the introduction to Isaiah at /study/bible/isaiah. State each view as its defenders would, and notice that the comfort stands on either view.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose that in the second session a woman in her fifties says she has prayed for six years for a son who no longer speaks to her, and that she has decided to stop, because hoping hurts more than not hoping. Before you can answer, someone quotes Isaiah 40:31 to her, warmly, and two others nod.

You will feel the pull to agree with the verse, or to defend her from it. Instead, read Isaiah 40:27 aloud, the exiles' own complaint, and point out that God kept their words in his book. Ask the group what it would look like to keep someone company in a long wait rather than hurry her out of it. Afterward, ask her privately whether she would like someone to pray with her for her son, or simply to remember him with her in January.

Use this to show that the verse is true and was never meant to be thrown at the weary. Ask the room which they have been.

sessions.title: Mary's Yes and Her Song
sessions.aim: To watch a young woman of no standing receive God's word with an honest question and full consent, and to hear her song as God's reversal of the proud and the humble, letting it fall first on our own side, and on ourselves, before we aim it at anyone else.
sessions.summary:
Mary has been painted so often that she is hard to see. Luke's Mary is a young woman in Nazareth, a village no earlier Scripture names, pledged in marriage to Joseph, a man of David's line, and living under Herod's rule. When the angel Gabriel greets her, she is "greatly troubled" (Luke 1:29). When he tells her she will bear the Son of the Most High, she asks how, since she is a virgin. Then she says yes: "I am the Lord's servant," Mary answered. "May it happen to me according to your word" (Luke 1:38). She said it though a pregnancy before the wedding could cost her dearly.

Then she sings of a God who "has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble" and "has filled the hungry with good things, but has sent the rich away empty" (Luke 1:52-53). It is an easy song to aim. Some hear a political manifesto against the powerful; others, a private song about humble hearts. Luke keeps both: real rulers, real hunger, real riches, and "those who are proud in the thoughts of their hearts" (Luke 1:51). This session asks the hardest question of Advent. If you can hear Mary's song and think first of someone else's fall, where does it fall on you?

keyScripture.why: Mary praises the God who looked on "the humble state of His servant" (Luke 1:48) and who reverses the world's order, scattering the proud, bringing down rulers, lifting the humble, filling the hungry, and sending the rich away empty. Luke aims the song at the proud heart as well as at thrones, so it falls on every side, and first on anyone who sings it as good news about someone else.

discussion.q: What picture of Mary did you grow up with: a figure in a nativity set, a mother honored in a Catholic or Orthodox friend's prayers, or almost nothing at all? How does it compare with the young woman in Luke 1:26-38?
discussion.behind: Surface the traditions in the room without debating them. Some have honored Mary all their lives; some were taught to say little about her. Let both feel welcome, and see Luke's Mary freshly: young, troubled, questioning, and brave. If her later honors come up, say that churches differ and point to the questions at the back.

discussion.q: Mary asks, "How can this be" (Luke 1:34), and then says, "I am the Lord's servant" (Luke 1:38). What did her yes cost her, and how is her question different from a doubt that refuses?
discussion.behind: Hold her question and her consent together. Her faith thinks and questions without demanding a sign, unlike Zechariah, who asked for proof (Luke 1:18). Help the room feel the cost: a betrothed woman found pregnant faced suspicion and divorce (Matthew 1:19), and she said yes before she knew what anyone would do.

discussion.q: Read Luke 1:51-53 aloud. When you hear "those who are proud," "rulers," and "the rich," whom do you picture? When you hear "the humble" and "the hungry," whom do you picture?
discussion.behind: Let people answer before you comment. Most of us put others on the scattered side of the song and ourselves on the lifted side. Notice that the first group Mary names is defined not by money or office but by "the thoughts of their hearts" (Luke 1:51). The fifth question comes back to this.

discussion.q: Some read Mary's song as a political manifesto; others as a song about private humility. What does each reading get right, and what does Luke keep that each leaves out?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge, so state both at their strongest. The first is right that the song names real thrones, hunger, and riches, as Jesus' woes on the rich do (Luke 6:20-26). The second is right that it begins in Mary's soul, names the proud heart first, and praises what God does instead of handing anyone a program. Luke keeps both.

discussion.q: Where does Mary's song fall on you, and on the people you usually agree with?
discussion.behind: Move to self-implication, and let it reach every side. The conservative who hears "rulers" (Luke 1:52) as a warning to secular elites and the progressive who hears "the rich" (Luke 1:53) as a warning about other people's money are making the same move. Read Luke 18:11. No one may answer by naming the other party. You go first.

objections.objection: Mary's song is about economics and political power. Turning it into a lesson on inner humility is how comfortable Christians have escaped it for centuries.
objections.response: Grant it its full strength. The song names thrones, hunger, and wealth, not only attitudes; Luke follows it with Jesus' warning, "woe to you who are rich, for you have already received your comfort" (Luke 6:24), and the church has often sung it in comfort while the hungry stayed hungry. But the first people Mary names are "those who are proud in the thoughts of their hearts" (Luke 1:51), and pride belongs to no single class or party. The song praises what God has done with his own arm; it doesn't hand the reversal to one faction to carry out against another, and history is full of people who scattered the proud and then sat down on the same thrones. Read as one side's program, the Magnificat becomes a new throne.

objections.objection: Mary's song is a beautiful act of personal worship. Bringing politics and money into it divides the church and misses the point.
objections.response: Grant what is right in this. The song is worship first, "My soul magnifies the Lord" (Luke 1:46), and the church has been divided by people who used Scripture as a partisan weapon. But the song won't stay indoors. Mary sings of rulers brought down and the rich sent away empty, echoing Hannah, who sang that the LORD "raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap" (1 Samuel 2:8), and Luke carries the same reversal into Jesus' preaching (Luke 6:20-26). To keep the song only in the heart is to escape the half of it that falls on the comfortable. What divides the church is not the song. It is the pride the song names, on every side.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If Mary's song were sung about you, which line would you hope to be in, and which line are you afraid you might be in?
sessions.practice: Pray Mary's song (Luke 1:46-55) each evening this week; Christians have sung it at evening prayer for centuries. Each day, notice one place where you were proud in the thoughts of your heart, and name one person or group you would be glad to see brought down; then pray for their good by name. Once this week, do one hidden act of mercy for someone in a low place, a meal, a visit, a bill quietly paid, and tell no one. At the end of the week, write down which line of the song was hardest to pray.
sessions.closingPrayer: Mighty One, holy is your name. You looked on the humble state of a young woman in a village no one noticed, and through her you came to us. We confess that we have been proud in the thoughts of our hearts, quick to name the rulers and the rich who are not us. Scatter our pride before you scatter anyone else's. Fill the hungry among us and empty the full, and give us Mary's courage to say yes to your word when it costs us something. In the name of her Son, Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.
reflection: When I hear Mary's song, where do I instinctively place myself, and why there?
What honest question would I bring to God, and what would it look like for me to say yes anyway?
Where am I proud in the thoughts of my heart about the people I disagree with?
sessions.teaching:
Mary has been painted and carved so often that she is hard to see. Luke sets two announcements side by side. The angel Gabriel comes first to Zechariah, an old priest burning incense in the holy place of the temple, and then to a young woman in Nazareth, a farming village no earlier Scripture had named, pledged in marriage to Joseph, a man of David's line. "Greetings, you who are highly favored! The Lord is with you" (Luke 1:28). Luke says she was "greatly troubled" (Luke 1:29). God's favor, in this story, feels less like a reward than like being found.

The promise is enormous. Her son "will be called the Son of the Most High," and "His kingdom will never end!" (Luke 1:32-33). This is Isaiah's child. Mary's answer is a real question: "How can this be," Mary asked the angel, "since I am a virgin?" (Luke 1:34). God's answer is his own creative act: "the power of the Most High will overshadow you" (Luke 1:35), the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the cloud of glory settling on the tabernacle. "For no word from God will ever fail" (Luke 1:37). The church confesses in its creeds that Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary, and Mary's own question shows it was no easier to believe then than now.

Then she says yes. "I am the Lord's servant," Mary answered. "May it happen to me according to your word" (Luke 1:38). Zechariah had asked for proof and was struck silent; Mary asked to understand and then consented. Her yes was costly: a betrothed woman found pregnant faced suspicion and divorce, and Joseph at first resolved to divorce her quietly because he "was unwilling to disgrace her publicly" (Matthew 1:19). She said yes before she knew what Joseph, her family, or her village would do, a servant's consent to a calling that would one day bring her to stand near a cross (John 19:25).

At Elizabeth's house she hears a beatitude: "Blessed is she who has believed that the Lord's word to her will be fulfilled" (Luke 1:45). A word of care belongs here. Some in this room have prayed for children for years or have lost pregnancies, and this chapter can land on them like an accusation. Luke calls Elizabeth and Zechariah "righteous in the sight of God" (Luke 1:6) long before they had a child, and their story is no promise that every faithful couple will have one. The care page at /help/infertility is there for anyone carrying that grief.

Then Mary sings. The Magnificat, named from its first word in Latin, is woven from older Scripture, above all Hannah's prayer (1 Samuel 2:1-10), and it moves from Mary's own soul to the shape of history. God "has looked with favor on the humble state of His servant" (Luke 1:48), and then: "He has performed mighty deeds with His arm; He has scattered those who are proud in the thoughts of their hearts. He has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble. He has filled the hungry with good things, but has sent the rich away empty" (Luke 1:51-53). The verbs are in the past tense, as though God has already done it, because in the child Mary carries, he has begun to.

The song has been aimed in two directions, and each aim catches something true. Some hear a political manifesto, and they are right that it names real thrones, real hunger, and real riches, as Jesus will in his woes on the rich (Luke 6:24). Others hear a song of inner humility, and they are right that it begins in Mary's soul, names the proud heart before any throne, and praises what God does rather than handing anyone a program. Luke keeps both. A Magnificat that is only about other people's power becomes a weapon. A Magnificat that is only about the inner life lets the comfortable sing it without a tremor.

That is the song's danger for all of us. The conservative Christian hears "rulers" (Luke 1:52) and thinks of secular elites; the progressive hears "the rich" (Luke 1:53) and thinks of other people's money. The educated miss their own contempt for the faith of the unschooled, and the churchgoer sings it in a warm sanctuary and assumes he is among the humble. Jesus told a parable to "some who trusted in their own righteousness and viewed others with contempt" (Luke 18:9), about a Pharisee who prayed, "God, I thank You that I am not like the other men" (Luke 18:11). Every tribe knows how to pray that prayer. "God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble" (1 Peter 5:5).

So the writer and the leader of this study have to stand inside it first. By the measure of the world Mary sang in, most of us are among the well fed, and most of us have been proud in the thoughts of our hearts about the people we disagree with. If you hear Mary's song and think first of someone else, you have found the proud heart she was singing about. The way to the lifted side of the song runs downward: "For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted" (Luke 18:14).

Mary's song is good news only to people willing to stand on its low side, and that is why it belongs in Advent. The question it leaves with us is not which party it condemns. It is whether we are humble enough to be filled.

scriptureStudy.note: God's announcement comes to a village Scripture had never named and a young woman of no standing, and her first response is trouble: she "wondered what kind of greeting this might be" (Luke 1:29).
Gabriel gathers Israel's royal hopes onto Mary's son: the throne of David promised in 2 Samuel 7:12-13 and the endless government of Isaiah 9:7. "His kingdom will never end!" (Luke 1:33).
Mary asks how, not whether, and God answers with his Spirit and the overshadowing power of the Most High. Faith here includes an honest question and does not end in one.

Elizabeth, filled with the Spirit, recognizes the unborn Lord and blesses Mary's faith: "Blessed is she who has believed that the Lord's word to her will be fulfilled" (Luke 1:45). The unborn Lord is recognized and welcomed by two women the world overlooked.

The song begins in God's regard for "the humble state of His servant" (Luke 1:48). Luke's word for her lowly state is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for Hannah's affliction when she prayed for a son (1 Samuel 1:11), and it can mean low social standing as well as humility.
The reversal is told in the past tense, as if already done, and the song ends in covenant memory, God "remembering to be merciful, as He promised to our fathers" (Luke 1:54-55).

Hannah's song is Mary's model: "He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap" (1 Samuel 2:8). Both songs come from women God looked on in their low estate, and both say the same hard thing: "for by his own strength shall no man prevail" (1 Samuel 2:9).

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, trace what the church has done with this song. In the last days before Christmas, the Western church has long sung it at evening prayer framed by the O Antiphons, centuries-old prayers that call on Christ by titles from the prophets, such as Root of Jesse, Key of David, and Emmanuel; the verses of the hymn O Come, O Come, Emmanuel were later drawn from them. In 1521 Martin Luther dedicated his commentary on the Magnificat to the young Prince John Frederick of Saxony, teaching a future ruler from a village woman's song how God regards the lowly and the mighty.

Then weigh the churches' long disagreement about Mary, described in the questions at the back. The Council of Ephesus in 431 confirmed the title God-bearer, in Greek Theotokos, as a claim about her Son: the one she bore is God. Ask whether a church can sing this song honestly without letting it reorder its budget, its friendships, and its politics.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose that ten minutes into this session a participant says the song is obviously about the politicians he can't stand, and names a few. Someone across the room bristles and answers that the people Mary meant are the ones he votes for. The temperature rises, and two people who usually sit together are looking at the floor.

You will feel the pull to shut the exchange down, or to settle who is right. Do neither. Read Luke 1:51 slowly and point out whom Mary names first: those who are proud in the thoughts of their hearts. Read Luke 18:11, the Pharisee's prayer of thanks that he was not like other men, and ask each person, yourself first, to say where the song falls on their own side. If feelings still run hot, close in prayer and follow up with each of them privately during the week.

Use this to show that Mary's song is no weapon for any party. Ask the group which they find easier to hear, the line about the rulers or the line about the proud heart.
