sessions.title: The Word Became Flesh
sessions.aim: To confess with John's Gospel and the Nicene Creed that the child of Christmas is the eternal Word who was with God and was God and who became flesh, and to see why the church would not let that confession be softened into sentiment or thinned into abstraction.
sessions.summary:
Christmas is easy to lose in two opposite directions. One makes it sentimental: a sweet baby, a stable, a feeling that asks nothing of anyone. The other makes it abstract: a doctrine for theologians with nothing to say to a Tuesday afternoon. John's Gospel opens with neither. It begins where Genesis begins: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). Then it says what no one could have guessed: "The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us" (John 1:14). The word for dwelling means pitching a tent, and it recalls the tabernacle in the wilderness, where God's glory filled the tent.

Early in the fourth century a popular teacher named Arius taught that the Son was the first and greatest of God's creatures, glorious but made. The church answered at Nicaea in 325 and at Constantinople in 381 with the creed many churches still confess, which calls the Son begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father, and says that for us and for our salvation he came down from heaven and was made man. If the Son were a creature, God would not have come for us himself. This session reads John's prologue and the creed together, and asks what it means for our bodies, and our neighbors', that God took a body and kept it.

keyScripture.why: John's prologue is one of the Bible's most direct statements of the incarnation. The Word who was with God and was God, through whom all things were made, "became flesh and made His dwelling among us" (John 1:14), pitching his tent where the glory once filled the tabernacle. The church's creeds guard what these verses confess.

discussion.q: When has Christmas felt merely sweet to you, and when has it felt too abstract to matter? Which way do you tend to lose it?
discussion.behind: Surface the two errors before the text corrects them. Some grew up with a Christmas that was all feeling, others with one that was all doctrine. Let people say which way they drift; the session will refuse both.

discussion.q: John begins "In the beginning," not in Bethlehem. Read John 1:1-5. What changes about the child in the manger when you hear who John says he is?
discussion.behind: Let the scale of the claim land. The child is the Word through whom "all things were made" (John 1:3), and the light that "shines in the darkness" (John 1:5) answers the first session's people in the dark. The manger is the Creator entering what he made.

discussion.q: Read John 1:14 alongside Exodus 40:34-35 and Exodus 33:18-20. What did Moses ask to see, and what does John mean when he says, "We have seen His glory" (John 1:14)?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge. The Word "made His dwelling" among us, literally pitched his tent, as the glory once filled the tabernacle. Moses was told no one could see God's face and live; John says the glory has been seen in one "full of grace and truth" (John 1:14), echoing Exodus 34:6. The invisible God has a face.

discussion.q: The church spent much of the fourth century arguing over whether the Son is of one substance with the Father. Why would it matter so much whether the Son is fully God rather than the greatest of creatures?
discussion.behind: Grant the skeptic's suspicion that this was hair-splitting, and that the key word isn't in Scripture. Then show the stakes: if the Son is a creature, God did not come himself, and the cross is someone else's suffering on his behalf. Read the creed aloud together from /resources/creeds/nicene-creed, and pause at the line about coming down for us and for our salvation.

discussion.q: If God took a body and kept it, what does that say about the bodies around you this December: the sick, the hungry, the aging, the grieving, your own? Where do we, and where does the church, prefer a God who keeps a safe distance?
discussion.behind: Move to self-implication and practice. The church has often confessed the incarnation while treating bodies as an afterthought, and both the abstract God and the sentimental one leave our lives untouched. Ask what one bodily act of care would look like this week, and go first.

objections.objection: The incarnation is a contradiction. Something can't be infinite and finite, God and man, at the same time. It's a beautiful idea, but it makes no sense.
objections.response: Grant what is fair. The incarnation is a mystery, and the creeds don't claim to explain how it works; the Council of Chalcedon in 451 drew boundaries around it rather than a diagram. But press on the charge of contradiction. The creed doesn't say that God turned into a man, or that God is both God and not God in the same sense. It says that one person, the eternal Son, took a full human nature into his life without ceasing to be what he always was. That is strange, but strange is not incoherent, and C. S. Lewis argued in Miracles that it is the central miracle, the one that makes sense of the rest. The question is finally historical: who was Jesus? Thomas, who would not believe without evidence, answered when he saw the risen Christ: "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:28).

objections.objection: The church turned a Galilean teacher into a god three centuries after his death. Jesus never claimed to be God; the councils invented it out of Greek philosophy.
objections.response: Grant what is true. The creed uses philosophical vocabulary that isn't in Scripture, and the councils were tangled up with emperors and politics. But the claims the creed protects are already in the New Testament, written within the first century. John says that the Word "was God" and that through him "all things were made" (John 1:1-3), giving Jesus the work of creation that Israel's faith reserved for God alone. Paul, writing within a few decades of the crucifixion, describes Christ as "existing in the form of God" (Philippians 2:6). The councils chose a word to guard that faith after the Bible's own phrases had been bent to make the Son less. You may reject the claim, but it wasn't added three centuries later.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Which is harder for you to believe, that God is great or that God came close? What would change if you believed the harder one?
sessions.practice: Read the Nicene Creed aloud once a day this week from /resources/creeds/nicene-creed, pausing at the line that confesses the Son came down from heaven for us and for our salvation. Once during the week, read John 1:1-14 aloud with someone else. And because God took a body and did not despise it, do one bodily act of care: visit someone sick or shut in, bring a meal, sit with someone in a nursing home, or let your own tired body rest without guilt. At the end of the week, write down what it was like to confess the incarnation and then act on it.
sessions.closingPrayer: Eternal Word, you were with God in the beginning, and through you all things were made. You came to your own, and your own did not receive you, and still you came. We confess that we have preferred you at a distance, because a God who comes close asks for our lives. Forgive us. We believe that you became flesh and pitched your tent among us, that you died and rose in the body, and that you will come again. Make us people who honor the bodies around us because you took one, and let us see your glory, full of grace and truth. Amen.
reflection: Do I tend to make Christmas sentimental or abstract, and what has that cost me?
What does it mean for me today that the invisible God has made himself known in Jesus?
Whose body around me, my own included, is God asking me to honor this week?
sessions.teaching:
Christmas is easy to lose in two directions. The first is sentiment: the baby in the manger becomes sweet and small, a figure who asks nothing of anyone. The second is abstraction: the incarnation becomes a doctrine argued over in old councils, with nothing to say to a hospital room. Both are comfortable. A sentimental God can be visited once a year, and an abstract God can be discussed without being met. The church's creeds are, among other things, a refusal to lose Christmas in either direction.

John's Gospel has no manger and no shepherds. It begins where the Bible begins: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). The Word was with God, distinct from the Father, and was God, sharing his nature, and "Through Him all things were made" (John 1:3). Then John takes up our first session's theme: "The Light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it" (John 1:5). So the light Isaiah promised to Galilee, which no king like Ahaz could have given, is the one through whom the stars were made.

John doesn't pretend the world was waiting with open arms. "He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him" (John 1:11). But to those who did receive him he gave the right to become children of God, "born not of blood, nor of the desire or will of man, but born of God" (John 1:13). The coming of the Word divides the world into those who shut the door and those who open it, and it doesn't consult anyone's family tree.

Then comes the sentence the whole faith turns on: "The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth" (John 1:14). Flesh is a hard word. John doesn't say the Word took on a human appearance; he says the Word became what we are, frail and mortal. Some early Christians found that too much to believe and taught that Jesus only seemed human, and the first letter of John draws the line: "Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God" (1 John 4:2). And the word for dwelling means to pitch a tent. When Israel's tent in the wilderness was finished, "the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle" (Exodus 40:34). John is saying that the glory has pitched its tent in a human body.

Moses once begged God, "Please show me Your glory," and was told, "You cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live" (Exodus 33:18-20). Then the LORD passed by and proclaimed himself "abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6), the pair John echoes in "full of grace and truth" (John 1:14). What Moses could not see, John says we have seen: "No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known" (John 1:18). For anyone who grew up without a father, or with one who did harm, this is no small thing: we are not left to guess what the Father is like from the fathers we had.

The church had to fight for this. Early in the fourth century Arius, a popular presbyter in Alexandria, taught that the Son was the first and greatest of God's creatures, glorious but made. In 325 the Council of Nicaea answered that the Son is of one substance with the Father, and in 381 the Council of Constantinople gave the creed the fuller form many churches still confess: the Son is Light of Light, very God of very God, begotten, not made, and for us and for our salvation he came down from heaven and was made man. Athanasius of Alexandria, exiled again and again for defending Nicaea, argued that only the Creator could renew his creation. Later in that century, when Apollinarius of Laodicea taught that in Christ the Word took the place of a human mind, Gregory of Nazianzus answered with a line the church has kept: what Christ did not take up, he did not heal.

A skeptic will say this is philosophy laid over a Galilean teacher, and that the creed's key word isn't in the Bible. That is fair. But the word was chosen to protect what the Bible says, after its own phrases had been bent to make the Son less than God, and the stakes were not academic. If the Son is a creature, God did not come for us himself; he sent someone else. The letter to the Hebrews says why it matters that he came in person: "He too shared in their humanity, so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death" (Hebrews 2:14).

And because God took a body and kept it, bodies matter. The sick, the hungry, the aging, the disabled, and the dying are not souls in temporary housing. We have to stand inside this too. The church has often confessed the incarnation on Sunday and treated bodies as an afterthought the rest of the week, and most of us prefer a God at a safe distance. A God who becomes flesh comes close enough to be refused, and close enough to ask for our hands.

Christmas is not God sending a message about himself. It is God arriving in person, as a baby who needed to be fed. The question John leaves with us is the one Christmas still leaves: whether we will receive him, or keep him at a distance where he cannot ask anything of us.

scriptureStudy.note: John begins where Genesis begins: the Word was God, and "without Him nothing was made that has been made" (John 1:3). The one in the manger made everything that exists.
Life and light belong to the Word, and "the darkness has not overcome it" (John 1:5). The light Isaiah promised to a people in darkness is the life of the Creator himself.
The world did not recognize its maker, and his own did not receive him. Those who did are given a new birth that depends on God, not on ancestry, effort, or human decision.

The Word became flesh, full human nature, and "made His dwelling among us," pitching his tent as God once lived among Israel in the tabernacle. The glory is now seen in a person "full of grace and truth" (John 1:14).
When the tabernacle was finished, "the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle," so that even Moses could not enter (Exodus 40:35). John's word for dwelling reaches back to this tent.

Moses asked to see God's glory and was told, "no one can see Me and live" (Exodus 33:20). Then God proclaimed himself "abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6), the pair John echoes in "grace and truth" (John 1:14).

No one has ever seen God, but the Son, "who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known" (John 1:18). The Greek verb behind made known gives us the word exegesis: the Son is the Father's own explanation.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, read Athanasius. His short fourth-century book On the Incarnation argues that when humanity, made in God's image, fell into corruption and death, only the Word through whom it was made could renew it, taking a body like ours so that death could be undone from the inside. Set beside it the Council of Chalcedon in 451, which confessed one person in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation, four negatives that fence the mystery rather than explain it. Then read the chapter of G. K. Chesterton's The Everlasting Man on the birth of Christ, which dwells on the paradox of the maker of the world born as a helpless child in a cave.

Ask whether our care for bodies and our patience with the suffering show that we believe what the church guarded so carefully. A doctrine of the incarnation that never reaches a hospital room has not yet been believed.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose that in this session a participant who works night shifts as a nurse says she can't connect with talk about one substance with the Father. What she sees all week is bodies failing, and some weeks she wonders whether God cares about bodies at all. A retired engineer across the room says, gently, that the creed sounds to him like a word game.

You will feel the pull to defend the creed with more vocabulary, or to drop it as too abstract. Do neither. Read John 1:14 and Hebrews 2:14-18 aloud. Point out that the church fought over that one word because it believed God himself came into flesh, the kind of flesh she cares for every night, and that a lesser Christ would mean God had kept his distance from her patients. Then ask the engineer what one wrong word can do to a structure meant to bear weight.

Use this to show that the creed and the hospital ward belong together. Ask the group where they most need to know that God took a body.

memoryVerse.text: The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.

sessions.title: He Will Come Again
sessions.aim: To recover Advent as the season of two comings, reading Paul's words to a grieving young church and John's vision of a new creation in their own settings, so that those who carry an empty chair into Christmas find a hope that does not deny their loss, and all of us learn to live between his first coming and his second.
sessions.summary:
Christmas can be the loneliest day of the year for people who are grieving, and the season's cheer can make sorrow feel like failure. Advent offers something truer, because it is more than a countdown to Christmas. It holds two comings, and many churches begin it each year not at the manger but with Jesus' words about his return.

Paul wrote his first letter to the Thessalonians around AD 50 or 51, to a church only months old, made up mostly of people who had turned from idols to the living God. Some of them had died, and the living were grieving, unsure what would become of their dead when the Lord came. Paul didn't tell them to stop grieving. He wrote "so that you will not grieve like the rest, who are without hope" (1 Thessalonians 4:13), and he grounded their hope in Jesus' death and resurrection and his coming again. Decades later John, on the island of Patmos, saw a new heaven and a new earth and heard that God "will wipe away every tear from their eyes" (Revelation 21:4). Christians differ about the timing of these things but agree that Christ will come, the dead will rise, and God will dwell with his people. This session asks how to keep Christmas between two comings, with a hope that has room for tears.

keyScripture.why: Paul writes to a young church grieving its dead. He doesn't forbid their grief; he gives it a floor: "since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, we also believe that God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in Him" (1 Thessalonians 4:14). He ends with comfort, not a timetable: "Therefore encourage one another with these words" (1 Thessalonians 4:18).

discussion.q: Who or what is missing from your Christmas this year? You're welcome to pass, or to answer for someone you love who is grieving.
discussion.behind: Make room for grief at the start, without fixing it. For some it is a person who has died; for others a marriage, a child at the other parent's house, or a parent with dementia. Let names be said aloud if people want to, and answer with thanks, not comfort.

discussion.q: Read 1 Thessalonians 4:13-14. What does Paul assume about grief, and what does he change?
discussion.behind: Paul assumes believers grieve. He forbids only grief "like the rest, who are without hope" (1 Thessalonians 4:13), in a world whose grave inscriptions often spoke of death as the end. What he offers is not fewer tears but a floor under them: Jesus died and rose, and those who belong to him will rise. Make sure no one leaves thinking a Christian shouldn't cry at Christmas.

discussion.q: Christians disagree about how the events of 1 Thessalonians 4:15-17 fit together and about the timing of Christ's return. Why do you think Paul ends with "encourage one another" (1 Thessalonians 4:18) rather than a timetable?
discussion.behind: Keep this from becoming a debate about the rapture. Name the main views briefly and fairly, as the primer does, and point to what Paul is doing: comforting grieving people. All who confess his return agree that he will come, the dead will rise, and "we will always be with the Lord" (1 Thessalonians 4:17).

discussion.q: Read Revelation 21:1-5. What does God do in this vision, and what does it mean that God himself "will wipe away every tear from their eyes" (Revelation 21:4)?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge. The movement is downward: the city comes down, and God makes his dwelling with people, the same tent word used of the Word made flesh (John 1:14). The tears are not declared unimportant. God's own hand wipes them away, which means they were real.

discussion.q: The Christmas story includes Rachel "weeping for her children, and refusing to be comforted" (Matthew 2:18). How can we keep Christmas so the grieving have room in it? Where have we, or the church, asked them to perform a joy they don't have?
discussion.behind: Move to self-implication and practice. Most of us have hurried a grieving person along because their sorrow interrupted our celebration. Talk about practical mercies: setting a place, saying a name, remembering them in January. You go first.

objections.objection: Talk of Jesus coming again is wishful thinking, a way for people who can't face death to pretend it isn't final.
objections.response: Grant the force of the suspicion. Karl Marx called religion the opium of the people, a painkiller that kept the suffering from changing their world, and churches have used heaven to excuse injustice and to hurry the grieving. Then look at what Paul wrote. He doesn't deny death or tell anyone not to grieve. His hope rests not on a feeling but on a claim about an event, "that Jesus died and rose again" (1 Thessalonians 4:14), which is true or false and can be weighed. The Thessalonians didn't hold this hope because it was easy; they received the message "in spite of your great suffering" (1 Thessalonians 1:6). And the hope doesn't sedate. It says this world matters enough to be judged and made new. You don't have to accept it to see that it isn't a painkiller.

objections.objection: Don't talk about heaven to grieving people at Christmas. It only tells them to stop being sad.
objections.response: Grant it, because it is often true. Telling a widow her husband is in a better place, in order to stop her tears, is not comfort; it asks her to make the rest of us comfortable. Jesus wept at the grave of a friend he was about to raise (John 11:35). But Paul gave this hope precisely to grieving people and told them to "encourage one another with these words" (1 Thessalonians 4:18). The answer is not silence about hope but honesty and timing. Grieve with them first and say the name. Then let hope be a promise they can lean their weight on, not a reason they must stop crying. Revelation's promise assumes tears that only God will wipe away.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: When you imagine the day God wipes away every tear, whose face do you see, and what would you most want to say to God about the waiting until then?
sessions.practice: This week, make room for grief at Christmas, yours or someone else's: set a place, light a candle, or say a name at the table. Read 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18 once this week and Revelation 21:1-5 on Christmas Day. Reach out to one person facing a first or second Christmas after a death, a divorce, or a move, with a call, a note, or an invitation that needs no answer. Each night, pray the prayer that closes the Bible: "Come, Lord Jesus!" (Revelation 22:20). If the season brings thoughts of not wanting to live, call or text 988 tonight, or call 911 if you are in danger, and tell someone you trust; the care pages at /help/grief and /help/loneliness are there for the days after.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, you came once in the dark, and you have promised to come again. Some of us carry an empty chair into this Christmas, and some of us have hurried others past their grief. Forgive us, and teach us to grieve with hope. We believe that you died and rose again, and that those who sleep in you will rise. We wait for the day when God will dwell with us and wipe away every tear, when death and mourning and crying and pain will be no more. Until then, keep us awake, keep us kind, and keep us waiting. Come, Lord Jesus. Amen.
reflection: Who is missing from my Christmas, and have I let myself grieve them with hope?
Do I long for Christ's return, or have I grown comfortable enough not to?
Whom could I make room for at my table, or in my attention, this Christmas?
sessions.teaching:
Christmas can be the loneliest day of the year for people who are grieving. The ornament made by a child who is gone comes out of its box, and the chair at the table stays empty. The culture's cheer makes sorrow feel like failure, and churches sometimes add to it: be joyful, they're in a better place. Advent offers something truer and harder, because it does not end at the manger.

Advent holds two comings at once: the first, which ended Israel's long wait in Bethlehem, and the second, which has not happened yet. That is why many churches that follow a lectionary begin Advent with Jesus' words about his return: "At that time they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory" (Luke 21:27). The Nicene Creed confesses that he shall come again with glory to judge the living and the dead. The letter to the Hebrews holds both comings in a single sentence: Christ "was offered once to bear the sins of many; and He will appear a second time, not to bear sin, but to bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him" (Hebrews 9:28).

Paul's first letter to the Thessalonians, written from Corinth around AD 50 or 51, is very likely the earliest of his letters to survive. He had founded the church only months before and left by night after a mob accused the believers of "saying that there is another king, named Jesus!" (Acts 17:7). The church he left behind was made up mostly of people who had "turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God and to await His Son from heaven" (1 Thessalonians 1:9-10). Then some of them died, and the living grieved, unsure what would become of their dead when the Lord came.

Paul doesn't forbid their grief. "Brothers, we do not want you to be uninformed about those who sleep in death, so that you will not grieve like the rest, who are without hope" (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Many grave inscriptions of that world spoke of death as the end. What Paul changes is the floor beneath the tears: "For since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, we also believe that God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in Him" (1 Thessalonians 4:14). He says plainly that Jesus died; those who belong to him fall asleep in him.

Then Paul describes the Lord's coming, the dead in Christ rising first, and the living "caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air" (1 Thessalonians 4:17). Faithful Christians read the sequence differently. Some expect believers to be caught up before a time of tribulation, since "God has not appointed us to suffer wrath" (1 Thessalonians 5:9). Others expect believers to rise and meet Christ at his one visible return, reading Paul's word for meeting as the one used when a city's citizens went out to welcome an arriving king and escort him in. This study leaves the timing open. What Paul cares about is plain: "And so we will always be with the Lord. Therefore encourage one another with these words" (1 Thessalonians 4:17-18). He gives the grieving a person, not a calendar, and the day itself will come "like a thief in the night" (1 Thessalonians 5:2).

John wrote Revelation to seven small churches under Rome's shadow, most likely late in the first century. He saw "a new heaven and a new earth," and the holy city "coming down out of heaven from God" (Revelation 21:1-2). The movement in John's vision is downward: God comes to live with his people. "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them" (Revelation 21:3), in the same tent word John's Gospel used when the Word became flesh. Then comes the promise the grieving need most: "He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the former things have passed away" (Revelation 21:4), words Isaiah first spoke of a feast on God's mountain (Isaiah 25:8). Christians differ about how much of this world carries over, but the creeds confess the resurrection of the body and the life of the world to come, not souls escaping matter.

The Christmas story itself doesn't hide grief. When Herod heard of a king born in Bethlehem, he killed the little boys of the town, and Matthew borrows Jeremiah's words for the mothers: "Rachel weeping for her children, and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more" (Matthew 2:18). The first coming did not end grief. It began its ending, and some sorrows will not be answered until the second. Paul's first letter to the Corinthians keeps one of the earliest Christian prayers in its Aramaic form, marana tha, which the Berean Standard Bible renders "Come, O Lord!" (1 Corinthians 16:22), and the Bible closes with the same longing: "Come, Lord Jesus!" (Revelation 22:20). The grieving often pray it more honestly than anyone.

We have to stand inside this as well. Most of us want the first coming without the second, a baby who will never judge anyone, but the creed won't allow it, and his coming is also a call to stay awake (1 Thessalonians 5:6). And the church has asked grieving people to perform a joy they didn't have and called it faith.

So keep Christmas between two comings. Light the candles and set the table, and leave room at it for grief. Say the names of the ones who are missing. Advent ends at Christmas, but the waiting does not. The child of Bethlehem will come again, and on that day God himself will wipe the tears from every face that is still waiting for him.

scriptureStudy.note: Paul assumes that believers grieve and forbids only grief "like the rest, who are without hope" (1 Thessalonians 4:13). The hope rests on an event: Jesus died and rose, and God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep in him.
The Lord descends, the dead in Christ rise, and the living are gathered to meet him. Paul's purpose is plain: "Therefore encourage one another with these words" (1 Thessalonians 4:18).

There is no timetable; the day comes "like a thief in the night" (1 Thessalonians 5:2). The waiting church stays awake and sober, wearing "the helmet of our hope of salvation" (1 Thessalonians 5:8), and they "encourage and build one another up" (1 Thessalonians 5:11).

Isaiah saw a feast for all peoples on God's mountain, where "He will swallow up death forever" and "The Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from every face" (Isaiah 25:8). The people say, "This is the LORD for whom we have waited" (Isaiah 25:9).
The city comes down and God dwells with people, the tent word of John 1:14. God wipes away the tears himself, and "there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain" (Revelation 21:4).

"Behold, I make all things new" (Revelation 21:5). The one on the throne promises renewal, not abandonment, and to the thirsty he will give "freely from the spring of the water of life" (Revelation 21:6).

The Christmas story includes a massacre and mothers "refusing to be comforted, because they are no more" (Matthew 2:18). Matthew tells it without softening, and the church may hold that grief and the joy of the birth together at Christmas.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, notice how much of the church's Advent looks toward the second coming. Many lectionaries assign Jesus' words about his return to the first Sunday of the season, and the Nicene Creed confesses his coming in glory in the same breath as his birth, death, and resurrection. Then weigh how faithful churches read the thousand years of Revelation 20: as a future reign of Christ on earth, as the present reign of Christ with his saints, or as a long age of the gospel's spread before his return.

Then ask what difference the second coming makes to the way we keep Christmas. The first coming shows that God keeps his word; the second promises that he will finish what he began. A church that longs for his return will treat the grieving, the poor, and the suffering as people whose story is not over, and it will not mistake the comforts of December for the kingdom it is waiting for.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose your last session falls on the Sunday after Christmas. A woman whose adult son died in the spring says she skipped the Christmas Eve service because she couldn't bear the singing, and then she apologizes for bringing the room down. Before you can answer, someone tells her kindly that her son is celebrating Christmas with Jesus and that she should try to be happy for him.

Don't correct that person in front of everyone, and don't let the moment pass. Thank her for telling the truth, and say plainly that she has nothing to apologize for. Read 1 Thessalonians 4:13 and Matthew 2:18, and point out that Scripture makes room for grief in the very season we are keeping. Afterward, ask her privately whether she has people around her through January, and make sure she knows about /help/grief and the eight-week plan at /plans/grief. If she says anything about not wanting to live, follow the leader primer that night.

Use this to show the difference between hope offered as a promise and hope used as a muzzle. Ask the group which they have received, and which they have given.

memoryVerse.text: ‘He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,’ and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the former things have passed away.

leaderPrimer:
December fills a room unevenly. Some in your group will arrive glad. Others will carry a first Christmas after a funeral, a marriage that ended this year, children spending the holiday at the other parent's house, a lost job, a bank balance that can't stretch to the gifts, or no family at all. The hazard of leading in Advent is the pressure to make the room festive, and to fix the people who aren't. Resist both. Let people be sad without apologizing and glad without feeling guilty, and don't hurry anyone to the manger.

Keep help within reach, because the holidays sharpen grief and strain fragile households. Before the first session, put these on a card on the table: the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988, free and confidential at any hour); the Crisis Text Line (text HOME to 741741); the National Domestic Violence Hotline (1-800-799-7233, or text START to 88788); and 911 whenever anyone is in immediate danger. The care pages at /help/grief, /help/loneliness, /help/divorce, and /help/money go further than a study can, and the eight-week plans at /plans/grief and /plans/loneliness can carry someone through January. You are not a counselor, and nothing in this guide is medical, legal, or financial advice. When someone's sadness lasts, or touches sleep, appetite, or work, encourage them to see a doctor or a counselor, and say plainly that doing so is not a failure of faith.

If anyone speaks of not wanting to live, of suicide, or of everyone being better off without them, take it seriously every time. Stop, thank them, talk with them privately as soon as you can, stay with them, and call or text 988 together; in immediate danger, call 911. If someone tells you they are being hurt, threatened, or controlled at home, believe them, and put their safety first, before reconciliation and before keeping the family together for the holidays. Never counsel anyone to stay in danger or to confront a violent person; the National Domestic Violence Hotline helps people make a safety plan at any hour. If a child is being harmed or neglected, the child's safety comes first; call the police or your state's child protective services. Church leaders may be mandated reporters of abuse and neglect, the laws vary by state, and you need to know your own obligations before the study begins. Never ask anyone to disclose danger, abuse, or thoughts of suicide in the group. When it comes out anyway, stop, talk privately, and connect them to help. Set the rule of confidentiality at the first meeting, and state its limit as plainly: you will not keep a secret that leaves someone in danger.

For households, point to the family Advent devotions at /family/devotions: a short reading for each day from December 1 to Christmas Day, each with a passage, a reflection, a question, and a prayer, and the whole set prints as a booklet in US Letter and A4.

Read Isaiah where Isaiah stood before you read him toward Christ. Isaiah 9 was first spoken to a frightened king and an occupied Galilee, and Isaiah 40 to exiles. The promises lose nothing by being heard first in their own century; they gain weight, and they keep faith with the skeptic in your room and with the Jewish people who first received them. Then follow the promise to Christ without embarrassment.

Some questions this study raises are open among faithful Christians, and the guide leaves them open. The first is how Isaiah 40 to 66 came to be. Some hold that Isaiah of Jerusalem received these chapters for a generation not yet born; they cite the New Testament, which quotes both halves of the book under his name (John 12:38-41), and their comfort is a God who announces events before they happen. Others hold that a prophet in Isaiah's tradition spoke chapters 40 to 55 near the end of the exile; they note chapters that name Cyrus as a present figure (Isaiah 44:28), and their comfort is a God whose word lived on among Isaiah's disciples (Isaiah 8:16). The second is how Isaiah's royal promises relate to Jesus: as a direct portrait of the Messiah, since "Mighty God" is used of the LORD himself (Isaiah 10:21), or as promises with a near horizon in Isaiah's own day, like the sign tied to Ahaz's crisis (Isaiah 7:16), that waited for their fullness in Christ. The first rests in a plan that always had Christ at its center; the second, in promises that keep their word in history and then exceed it. The third is Mary. Catholic and Orthodox Christians honor her with titles and ask for her prayers, pointing to her own words in Luke 1:48, and their churches teach that she remained a virgin all her life; their comfort is a mother in the faith who prays for them. Protestants honor her as the model disciple and do not pray to her, pointing to Jesus' reply in Luke 11:27-28 and, most of them, to his brothers and sisters (Mark 6:3); their comfort is direct access to God through Christ alone. The fourth is the timing of Christ's return. Some hold that believers will be caught up before a time of tribulation, since "God has not appointed us to suffer wrath" (1 Thessalonians 5:9), and they take comfort in a Lord who spares his people; others hold that believers rise to meet him at his one visible return, as citizens went out to welcome a king, and they take comfort in a single public hope for the whole church. Christians also read the thousand years of Revelation 20 in more than one way. The fifth is whether to keep Advent at all, which the questions at the back take up. State each position as its defenders would, and let people disagree and remain brothers and sisters. Faithful churches differ, and James Bell's own landing on these questions is not given here.

Hold the floor while you leave those questions open. The historic creeds confess that Jesus Christ is true God and true man, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary, crucified, risen in the body, and coming again in glory to judge the living and the dead. The study states these as the church's confession, not as positions up for a vote, and it treats those who doubt them with patience. And keep Advent from becoming a culture war; the yearly quarrel over holiday greetings is not this study's subject.

Lead from inside the season. You don't need to have suffered what others in the room have suffered, but you do need to be honest that you, too, have trusted what you could see, grown tired of waiting, and wanted a Christmas that asked nothing of you. Five sessions won't lift anyone's darkness by Christmas. They can keep people company in it, and point them to the light the darkness has not overcome.

faq.q: What is Advent, and why wait for something that has already happened?
faq.a: Advent is the season of four Sundays before Christmas that many churches keep as a time of waiting. Its name comes from the Latin adventus, a coming, and it holds two comings at once: the first, which ended Israel's long wait in Bethlehem, and the second, which has not happened yet. That is why many churches begin Advent with Jesus' words about his return (Luke 21:25-28). As the letter to the Hebrews puts it, Christ "was offered once to bear the sins of many; and He will appear a second time, not to bear sin, but to bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him" (Hebrews 9:28).

faq.q: Our church has never kept Advent. Is it biblical, or only tradition?
faq.a: Faithful churches answer this differently, and the study leaves it open. Scripture gives no command to keep Advent. Those who keep it receive the church year as a gift, a yearly walk through the life of Christ, and they point to Paul: "He who observes a special day does so to the Lord" (Romans 14:6). Those who don't keep it hold that the Lord's Day is the one holy day Scripture gives the church, worry that other seasons can harden into law or into a show, and point to the letter to the Colossians: "let no one judge you by what you eat or drink, or with regard to a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath" (Colossians 2:16). Both can stand on Paul's rule: "Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind" (Romans 14:5). The study can be used either way.

faq.q: December is the hardest month of the year for me. Is this study for me?
faq.a: Yes, and it may be more for you than for anyone. Advent begins in the dark on purpose. It doesn't ask you to feel festive, and its Scriptures are full of people who waited and grieved and were not comforted quickly. Come as you are, and say as much or as little as you want. The care pages at /help/grief and /help/loneliness go further than a study can. If the season brings thoughts of not wanting to live, call or text 988 tonight, or call 911 if you are in danger, and tell someone you trust.

faq.q: Did Isaiah predict Jesus, or did Christians read Jesus back into Isaiah?
faq.a: It's a fair question, and it is why this study reads Isaiah in his own century first. Jewish interpreters have read the child of Isaiah 9 as a king of Isaiah's own day or as the Messiah still to come, and Christians differ about how much Isaiah's first hearers understood. Faithful readers also differ about whether Isaiah 40 came through Isaiah himself or a prophet in his tradition; the introduction at /study/bible/isaiah sets out the views. Two things are worth weighing. The names in Isaiah 9:6 outrun any king Judah ever had, and "Mighty God" is used of the LORD himself (Isaiah 10:21). And the New Testament doesn't claim that Isaiah ignored his own day; it claims that the light he promised to Galilee began to shine there in Jesus (Matthew 4:12-17). You don't have to accept that claim to see that it isn't careless.

faq.q: Do Christians have to believe in the virgin birth?
faq.a: The historic creeds confess that Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary, and this study holds that confession. Many find it hard: it is a claim about a miracle, Mark, John, and Paul don't describe it, and the Hebrew word in Isaiah 7:14 can mean simply a young woman. Those who hold the confession answer that Matthew and Luke tell the story independently and agree on its essentials, that Jewish Christians would hardly have invented a story that exposed Mary to scandal, and that the conception is told as God's creative act, nothing like the pagan tales of gods and women. Mary herself found it hard: "How can this be," Mary asked the angel, "since I am a virgin?" (Luke 1:34). The study asks you to see what the church was protecting: that Jesus is fully human, born of a woman, and the eternal Son, whose life did not begin in her womb.

faq.q: Catholics, Orthodox, and Protestants think differently about Mary. Where does this study stand?
faq.a: It honors Mary as Luke does, as the servant who believed God's word, and it doesn't settle the long disagreement among churches about her. Catholic and Orthodox Christians honor her with titles and ask for her prayers, pointing to her own words, "From now on all generations will call me blessed" (Luke 1:48), and their churches teach that she remained a virgin all her life. Protestants honor her as the model disciple and do not pray to her, pointing to Jesus' reply when a woman praised his mother (Luke 11:27-28), and most read his brothers and sisters (Mark 6:3) as Mary's later children. The Council of Ephesus in 431 confirmed the title God-bearer, which is first a claim about her Son: the one she bore is God. Churches that use the title and churches that avoid it can agree on that.

faq.q: Will there be a rapture? When will Jesus come back?
faq.a: No one knows when. Jesus said, "No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father" (Matthew 24:36). How the events of 1 Thessalonians 4:15-17 fit together is a question faithful Christians answer differently. Many dispensational Christians hold that believers will be caught up before a time of tribulation, since "God has not appointed us to suffer wrath" (1 Thessalonians 5:9); many other Christians hold that the gathering happens at Christ's one visible return, reading Paul's word for meeting as the welcome citizens gave an arriving king. All of them confess with the creed that he will come again in glory, that the dead in Christ will rise, and that "we will always be with the Lord" (1 Thessalonians 4:17). The study leaves the timing open.

faq.q: What do we say to someone who is grieving at Christmas?
faq.a: Less than you think, and later than you want to. Say their person's name, and let them talk about the one they miss. Don't tell them their loved one is in a better place in order to stop their tears, or that everything happens for a reason. Jesus wept at the grave of a friend he was about to raise (John 11:35), and Paul wrote to grieving believers "so that you will not grieve like the rest, who are without hope" (1 Thessalonians 4:13), not so that they would stop grieving. Invite them without pressure, and remember them in January, when the cards stop. If grief turns into talk of not wanting to live, stay with them and call or text 988 together. The care page at /help/grief has more.

faq.q: I'm not a believer. Is there a place for me in this study?
faq.a: Yes. Advent may be the most honest part of the Christian year, because it begins by admitting that the world is dark. You're welcome to listen, to ask hard questions, and to disagree. The study won't pretend its claims are small: that a promise spoken to a frightened king came true in Galilee, that the child of Bethlehem was God made flesh, and that he will come again to make all things new. It asks only that you weigh them, and it will try to state your objections as well as you would.

faq.q: How can our household keep Advent without adding one more thing to December?
faq.a: Keep it small, and let it subtract before it adds. Many households light one more candle each Sunday of Advent, read a short passage at dinner, and hold back some celebrating until Christmas itself. The family Advent devotions at /family/devotions give a short reading for each day from December 1 to Christmas Day and print as a booklet. None of it is required, and none of it earns anything. If December is already full, choose one practice and drop one obligation.

timeline.event: Isaiah son of Amoz receives his call "In the year that King Uzziah died" (Isaiah 6:1), as Assyria under Tiglath-pileser III (reigned 745 to 727 BC) becomes the dominant empire.
The kings of Aram and Israel march on Jerusalem. Against Isaiah's counsel, King Ahaz sends the temple's silver and gold to Tiglath-pileser and asks for his protection (Isaiah 7; 2 Kings 16:5-9).
Tiglath-pileser annexes Galilee, including the land of Naphtali, and deports its people (2 Kings 15:29), and in 732 BC takes Damascus. Isaiah 9 promises that a great light will rise on these lands.
Samaria falls to Assyria, ending the northern kingdom of Israel.
Babylon destroys Jerusalem and its temple and carries many of its people into exile. Lamentations grieves a city with no one to comfort her.
Cyrus of Persia takes Babylon, and in 539 or 538 BC he allows the exiles to return home. Isaiah 40 to 55 speak into the last years of the exile.

Jesus is born in Bethlehem in the last years of Herod the Great, whose death is usually dated to 4 BC (Matthew 2:1; Luke 1:5). His parents present him in the temple, where Simeon and Anna have been waiting (Luke 2:22-38).
Paul writes 1 Thessalonians from Corinth to a church only months old, comforting believers who grieve their dead (1 Thessalonians 4:13-18). It is very likely the earliest of his letters to survive.

John, on the island of Patmos, writes Revelation to seven churches in the Roman province of Asia, closing with a vision of a new heaven and a new earth (Revelation 21:1-5). A significant minority of scholars date it to the late 60s.
The Council of Nicaea confesses that the Son is of one substance with the Father, against Arius, who taught that the Son was the first and greatest of God's creatures.
The Council of Constantinople gives the Nicene Creed the form many churches still confess, including its confession that Christ will come again in glory.
The Council of Ephesus confirms the title God-bearer (Theotokos) for Mary, affirming that the one she bore is one person, truly God.
Martin Luther publishes a commentary on the Magnificat, dedicated to the young Prince John Frederick of Saxony, as a lesson in how God regards the lowly and the mighty.
From Tegel prison in Berlin, Dietrich Bonhoeffer writes late in the year that a prison cell, whose door opens only from outside, is not a bad picture of Advent.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome. Thank you for coming, especially if December is hard for you this year. A few things before we start. What's said in this room stays in this room, with one exception: if someone is in danger of harming themselves or someone else, or a child is being harmed, I won't keep that secret, and I may be required to get help. No one has to share anything; you're welcome to listen the whole time. Some of us come into this season full of joy, and some of us find it the hardest month of the year, and both belong here. Advent is a season of waiting, so we won't hurry to a happy ending tonight. Tonight we're looking at this together: ________. Let me read our passage, and then we'll sit with it a moment before anyone speaks.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked at what this passage meant when it was first spoken. Now let's bring it into this December, into the kitchens and hospital rooms, the empty chairs and crowded calendars where we're actually living, because that's where it either matters or it doesn't.
facilitatorScript.close: We'll stop there, even though Advent hasn't finished its work and neither has God. If tonight stirred up something heavy, please talk with me afterward, or with someone you trust this week. If you're in danger or thinking about ending your life, call or text 988, or call 911 in an emergency, and tell someone. Try the practice if you can, and remember that what was said here stays here. Let me pray for us before we go.

cadences.name: Through Advent (5 sessions)
plan: First week of Advent: Session 1, A People in the Dark, beginning with the ground rules, the card of help lines, and a word about the two comings.
Second week of Advent: Session 2, Comfort, and the Long Wait.
Third week of Advent: Session 3, Mary's Yes and Her Song.
Fourth week of Advent: Session 4, The Word Became Flesh, reading the Nicene Creed aloud together.
Christmas, or during the twelve days of Christmas before Epiphany on January 6: Session 5, He Will Come Again.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Explain Advent and the two comings, set the ground rules on confidentiality and its limits, hand out the card of help lines, and point households to /family/devotions.
Week 2: Session 1, with extended time on Isaiah 7 and 2 Kings 16 and the world under Assyria.
Week 3: Session 2, part one: Isaiah 40, the exile, and comfort that rests on pardon.
Week 4: Session 2, part two: Simeon and Anna, and the practice of waiting.
Week 5: Session 3, Mary's Yes and Her Song.
Week 6: Session 4, The Word Became Flesh.
Week 7: Session 5, He Will Come Again, with unhurried time for those who are grieving.
Week 8: Integration. Revisit the memory verses and practices, and decide together how the group will watch over one another through January.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Session 1, with the ground rules and help lines set at the start.
Week 4: Sessions 4 and 5 together, or Session 4 alone, with Session 5 held during the twelve days of Christmas.

bibliography.title: On the Incarnation
bibliography.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
bibliography.note: A short fourth-century treatise arguing that when humanity, made in God's image, fell into corruption and death, only the Word through whom it was made could renew it, and that he took a body like ours to overcome death from within. The theological spine of session 4.

bibliography.title: Miracles
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: Published in 1947. Its chapter The Grand Miracle argues that the incarnation is the central Christian miracle, the one that makes sense of the rest. Supports session 4.

bibliography.title: The Everlasting Man
bibliography.author: G. K. Chesterton
bibliography.note: Published in 1925. Its chapter The God in the Cave, which opens the book's account of Christ, dwells on the paradox of the Creator born as a helpless child in a cave. Supports session 4.

bibliography.title: Letters and Papers from Prison
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: Letters written after Bonhoeffer's arrest in 1943, edited by his friend Eberhard Bethge and published after his execution in 1945. One letter from late 1943 compares a prison cell, whose door opens only from outside, to Advent. Supports session 2.

bibliography.title: Advent: The Once and Future Coming of Jesus Christ
bibliography.author: Fleming Rutledge
bibliography.note: Published in 2018. Sermons and essays arguing that Advent begins in the darkness of the world as it is and looks toward Christ's second coming, not only toward Christmas. Background for sessions 1 and 5.

bibliography.title: The Magnificat
bibliography.author: Martin Luther
bibliography.note: A commentary on Mary's song published in 1521 and dedicated to the young Prince John Frederick of Saxony, teaching a future ruler from the song how God regards the lowly and the mighty. Background for session 3.

bibliography.title: The Birth of the Messiah
bibliography.author: Raymond E. Brown
bibliography.note: First published in 1977. A detailed commentary on the infancy narratives of Matthew and Luke and their Old Testament background, including the Magnificat and Simeon's song. Background for sessions 2 and 3.

bibliography.title: The Prophecy of Isaiah
bibliography.author: J. Alec Motyer
bibliography.note: A commentary that reads Isaiah as the unified work of the eighth-century prophet and treats the royal promises of chapters 7 to 11 and the comfort of chapter 40 as genuine prophecy. Represents the traditional view described in sessions 1 and 2.

bibliography.title: The Prophetic Imagination
bibliography.author: Walter Brueggemann
bibliography.note: Published in 1978. Argues that Israel's prophets formed an alternative to the royal consciousness of kings and empires, criticizing it through grief and energizing God's people through hope, as in the exile poetry of Isaiah 40 to 55. Background for sessions 2 and 3.

bibliography.title: The Theology of the Book of Revelation
bibliography.author: Richard Bauckham
bibliography.note: Published in 1993. Reads Revelation as prophecy, apocalypse, and a letter to seven churches, unmasking Rome's claims to power and ending in a new creation where God dwells with his people. Background for session 5.

bibliography.title: Surprised by Hope
bibliography.author: N. T. Wright
bibliography.note: Argues that the Christian hope is bodily resurrection in a renewed creation rather than souls leaving the earth for heaven, and reads Paul's picture of meeting the Lord in the air against the custom of citizens going out to welcome an arriving ruler, a reading that Christians who expect a rapture before the tribulation dispute. Background for session 5.

furtherReading: On the Incarnation, Athanasius of Alexandria, for anyone who wants to know why the church insisted that the child of Bethlehem is fully God, in a short book Christians have read for more than sixteen centuries.
Advent: The Once and Future Coming of Jesus Christ, Fleming Rutledge, for readers who want Advent's darkness and its hope of Christ's return taken seriously.
Letters and Papers from Prison, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, for anyone waiting in a place they cannot leave.
The Magnificat, Martin Luther, for anyone who wants to hear Mary's song as a word to the powerful and the proud, the proud in the church included.
Surprised by Hope, N. T. Wright, for the grieving and the curious who want a careful account of the hope of resurrection.

glossary.definition: From the Latin adventus, a coming. The season of four Sundays before Christmas in which many churches remember Israel's long wait for the Messiah and wait for Christ's coming again.
The return of Jesus Christ in glory, confessed in the creeds, when the dead will be raised and the world judged and made new. Christians differ about its timing, not about the promise.
The empire of northern Mesopotamia that dominated Isaiah's world. Under Tiglath-pileser III (reigned 745 to 727 BC) it annexed Galilee, and in 722 BC it ended the northern kingdom of Israel.
The decades many of Judah's people spent in Babylonia after Jerusalem fell in 587 or 586 BC, until Cyrus let them return in 539 or 538 BC.
A Hebrew name meaning God with us, given as a sign to the house of David in King Ahaz's crisis (Isaiah 7:13-14) and applied by Matthew to Jesus (Matthew 1:23).
From a Hebrew word meaning anointed one; Christ is the Greek equivalent. The hoped-for king from David's line whom Isaiah 9 and 11 describe and the New Testament confesses in Jesus.
Mary's song in Luke 1:46-55, named from its first word in Latin, magnifies, and sung at evening prayer for centuries.
Simeon's prayer in Luke 2:29-32, named from its first words in Latin, now you dismiss, and prayed by many churches at the close of the day.
From the Latin for taking flesh. The eternal Son of God taking a full human nature, body and soul, without ceasing to be God (John 1:14).
John's title for the Son in John 1:1-18, translating the Greek logos: God's own self-expression, through whom all things were made, who became flesh.

The confession drafted at the Council of Nicaea in 325 and given its fuller form at Constantinople in 381, confessing the Son as of one substance with the Father. The full text is at /resources/creeds/nicene-creed.
The creed's phrase, homoousios in Greek, for the Son's full equality with the Father: the same God, not a lesser one, against Arius, who taught that the Son was a creature.
In Greek, Theotokos, the title for Mary confirmed at the Council of Ephesus in 431. It is first a claim about Jesus: the one Mary bore is God.
A common name for the gathering of believers to meet the Lord in 1 Thessalonians 4:17, from the Latin verb the Vulgate used for caught up. Christians differ about its timing.
The Bible's hope for the end of the story: not souls escaping the world but a new heaven and a new earth where God dwells with his people and death is no more (Revelation 21:1-5).

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: December fills up fast, and for many people it is the hardest month of the year. This Advent, join Waiting for the Light, a five-session study for the Sundays of Advent and Christmas: Isaiah's promise of light to a people in the dark, Simeon's long wait, Mary's song, the Word made flesh, and the hope of Christ's coming again for everyone who carries an empty chair into Christmas. No one has to be festive, and no one has to share. Come as you are, glad or grieving.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: This Advent we're starting a five-session study called Waiting for the Light, one session for each Sunday of Advent and one for Christmas. It isn't about getting into the holiday spirit. Advent begins in the dark on purpose, and this study makes room for people who find December hard, the grieving, the lonely, those whose families have come apart this year, and those who are simply tired. No one has to share anything, and what people do share will be treated with care. Sign up at the welcome table, or talk with me afterward.
promoKit.inviteCaption: "The people walking in darkness have seen a great light" (Isaiah 9:2). Waiting for the Light is a five-session Advent study for anyone who finds December hard, and anyone who wants it to mean more. Come as you are.
quoteCards: Advent was made for people in the dark. It doesn't ask anyone to feel festive.
The light Isaiah promised rose in the very land that had gone dark.
God's comfort goes to the wound and speaks there.
Simeon waited for the consolation of Israel, and then he held it in his arms.
If you hear Mary's song and think first of someone else, you have found the proud heart she was singing about.
Christmas is not God sending a message. It is God arriving, as a baby who needed to be fed.
Hope is not a reason to stop crying. It is a floor under the tears.
Advent ends at Christmas. The waiting doesn't, and neither does the promise.
